steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a survey of deep multimodal representation learning: what multimodal systems are, how task-specific methods gave way to pretraining and unified architectures, and what the survey covers.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Multimodal vs cross-modal systems
- Multimodal representation learning
- From task-specific methods to pretraining
- What this survey covers

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Multimodal vs cross-modal systems
  - multimodal: two or more input modalities (audio, text, images, video) -> output modality, maybe different
  - cross-modal: subpart; one modality's information enhances the other
  - e.g. multimodal: image + text to assess a situation / perform a task; cross-modal: image -> text
  - examples: AVSR, detecting propaganda in memes, VQA
- Multimodal representation learning
  - reduces heterogeneity gap; processes raw heterogeneous data hierarchically
  - heterogeneous features -> additional semantics as contextual information
  - complementary information across modalities; e.g. lip motion helps speech recognition in AVSR
  - recent deep learning variants: classical challenges (correlation, translation, alignment, fusion) by mapping to a standard representation space
- From task-specific methods to pretraining
  - past: task-specific deep learning strategies improved many multimodal tasks
  - recently: pre-training / fine-tuning in NLP and CV get attention; semantically rich representations, large-scale public models
- What this survey covers
  - pipeline of task-specific methods for multimodal representation
  - pretraining types and pretext tasks for robust pretrained models on multimodal / cross-modal downstream tasks
  - most pretraining methods use transformers -> unifying architectures
  - unified models handle all modalities and tasks; no per-task fine-tuning; less computation and processing time
  - evaluation on downstream tasks, multimodal benchmarks, applications (sentiment analysis, document understanding, fake news detection, retrieval, translation, reasoning)
  - Figure 1: categorical percentage of surveyed papers; bar graph of yearly development / availability on Google Scholar

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multimodal systems use two or more input modalities, like audio, text, images or video, to produce an output modality, which could be different from the inputs. Cross-modal systems are a subpart of multimodal systems, and they use information from one modality to enhance the performance in the other modality. For example, a multimodal system would use image and textual modalities to assess a situation and perform a task, while a cross-modal system would use an image modality to output a textual modality. Examples of multimodal systems are Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR), detecting propaganda in memes, and Visual Question Answering (VQA).

Multimodal representation learning techniques reduce the heterogeneity gap between the different modalities by processing the raw heterogeneous data hierarchically. The heterogeneous features from different modalities offer additional semantics in the form of contextual information. So complementary information can be learned through multiple modalities. For example in AVSR the visual modality can help speech recognition by providing lip motion. Recent advanced variants of deep learning approaches have addressed the classical multimodal challenges (correlation, translation, alignment, fusion) by mapping the different modalities into a standard representation space.

- From task-specific methods to pretraining
  - past: task-specific deep learning strategies improved many multimodal tasks
  - recently: pre-training / fine-tuning in NLP and CV get attention; semantically rich representations, large-scale public models

- What this survey covers
  - pipeline of task-specific methods for multimodal representation
  - pretraining types and pretext tasks for robust pretrained models on multimodal / cross-modal downstream tasks
  - most pretraining methods use transformers -> unifying architectures
  - unified models handle all modalities and tasks; no per-task fine-tuning; less computation and processing time
  - evaluation on downstream tasks, multimodal benchmarks, applications (sentiment analysis, document understanding, fake news detection, retrieval, translation, reasoning)
  - Figure 1: categorical percentage of surveyed papers; bar graph of yearly development / availability on Google Scholar

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multimodal systems use two or more input modalities, like audio, text, images or video, to produce an output modality, which could be different from the inputs. Cross-modal systems are a subpart of multimodal systems, and they use information from one modality to enhance the performance in the other modality. For example, a multimodal system would use image and textual modalities to assess a situation and perform a task, while a cross-modal system would use an image modality to output a textual modality. Examples of multimodal systems are Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR), detecting propaganda in memes, and Visual Question Answering (VQA).

Multimodal representation learning techniques reduce the heterogeneity gap between the different modalities by processing the raw heterogeneous data hierarchically. The heterogeneous features from different modalities offer additional semantics in the form of contextual information. So complementary information can be learned through multiple modalities. For example in AVSR the visual modality can help speech recognition by providing lip motion. Recent advanced variants of deep learning approaches have addressed the classical multimodal challenges (correlation, translation, alignment, fusion) by mapping the different modalities into a standard representation space.

In the past, many task-specific deep learning strategies have enhanced the performance significantly for a variety of multimodal tasks. More recently, pre-training and fine-tuning methods for Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer Vision (CV) have got a lot of attention, mainly because of their semantically rich representation and because large-scale public models are available.

This study summarized the pipeline of the task-specific methods for multimodal representation. We discuss the pretraining types and the pretext task that are needed to make the pretrained model robust on a variety of multimodal or cross-modal downstream tasks. We show that most pretraining methods leverage transformers, and this leads to the inception of unifying architectures. These models can handle all modalities across diverse downstream tasks, so they reduce the need for individual task-specific fine-tuning, and this reduces both the computational complexity and the processing time. We also comprehensively present the evaluation on downstream tasks, the multimodal benchmarks, and an extensive range of multimodal applications, including NLP tasks that are enriched by adding visual and audio modalities, e.g., sentiment analysis, document understanding, fake news detection, retrieval, translation, and other reasoning applications. Figure 1 shows the categorical percentage of the deep learning multimodal papers included in this survey. The bar graph shows the development and the availability of deep learning multimodal approaches on Google Scholar per year.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Multimodal systems use two or more input modalities, such as audio, text, images, or video to produce an output modality, which could be different from the inputs. Cross-modal systems, a subpart of multimodal systems, utilize information from one modality to enhance the performance in the other modality. For example, a multimodal system would use image and textual modalities to assess a situation and perform a task, while a cross-modal system would use an image modality to output a textual modality [1,2]. Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR) [3], detecting propaganda in memes [4], and Visual Question Answering (VQA) [5] are examples of the multimodal systems. Multimodal representation learning techniques reduce the heterogeneity gap between different modalities by processing raw heterogeneous data hierarchically [6]. Heterogeneous features from different modalities offer additional semantics in the form of contextual information [6]. So complementary information can be learned through multiple modalities. For example, the visual modality can help speech recognition by providing lip motion [7] in the AVSR. Recent advanced variants of deep learning approaches have addressed classical multimodal challenges (correlation, translation, alignment, fusion) by mapping different modalities into a standard representation space.

In the past, many task-specific deep learning strategies have significantly enhanced the performance for a variety of multimodal tasks [8]. More recently, pre-training and fine-tuning methods for Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer Vision (CV) have received significant attention, mainly due to their semantically rich representation and the availability of large-scale public models [9]. This study summarized the pipeline of the task-specific methods for multimodal representation. We discuss pretraining types and pretext task required to make the pretrained model robust on the variety of multimodal or cross-modal downstream tasks. We show that most pretraining methods leverage transformers, leading to the inception of unifying architectures. These models, capable of handling all modalities across diverse downstream tasks, mitigate the need for individual task-specific fine-tuning, thereby reducing both computational complexity and processing time [10]. Additionally, evaluation on downstream tasks, multimodal benchmarks, extensive range of multimodal applications, including NLP tasks that are enriched by the incorporation of visual and audio modalities, e.g., sentiment analysis, document understanding, fake news detection, retrieval, translation, and other reasoning applications are comprehensively presented in this survey. Figure 1 shows the categorical percentage of deep learning multimodal papers included in this survey. The bar graph shows the development and the availability of deep learning multimodal approaches on Google Scholar yearly.
